Heat treatment of SLM-printed maraging steel transforms the as-built fine martensitic microstructure by promoting precipitate formation, relieving residual stresses, and—under intercritical conditions—reversing martensite to austenite, with corresponding changes in hardness and corrosion-related behavior. (Tan et al. 2018)

Microstructure of the as-built state: SLM produces a very fine martensitic matrix with submicron grains and a nearly fully dense part structure. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Precipitation and age hardening: Aging causes formation of massive needle-shaped nanoprecipitates Ni3X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) inside the martensitic matrix, which are responsible for age hardening through Orowan and coherency-strain mechanisms. (Tan et al. 2018)

Residual stress and anisotropy: Heat treatments significantly relieve residual stresses introduced by SLM and can slightly reduce the layer-wise mechanical anisotropy of printed parts. (Tan et al. 2018)

Reversed austenite formation: Intercritical tempering near the α' + γ range (example: 720°C) precipitates reversed austenite preferentially along martensite lath boundaries, driven by local Ni enrichment from dissolution of intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022)

Effects on hardness and measured properties: Aging yields maximum nano-hardness in SLM maraging steel, and heat treatment broadly aligns nano-hardness of SLM and wrought material in heat-treated conditions. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Tan et al. 2018)

Implications for surface/thermochemical treatments: Prior heat treatments alter the response to subsequent processes such as plasma nitriding, where untreated material produced cracked compound layers but prior aging/solution treatments led to improved nitrided-layer morphology and better wear and corrosion resistance. (Godec et al. 2021)

Mechanistic overview from reviews: AM intrinsically induces in situ tempering and precipitation phenomena in PH/maraging steels, producing hierarchical subgrains and fine precipitates that change strength, wear and corrosion behaviour compared to conventionally produced steels. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

### What these sources do not cover
Quantitative kinetics of specific precipitate evolution during defined heat-treatment cycles is not detailed in these passages.

(Khan et al. 2022) Studies report that reversed austenite formed by intercritical tempering improves pitting resistance relative to as-printed, aged, and homogenized specimens that lack reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022)

Aging of SLM maraging steel produces dense distributions of needle-shaped nanoprecipitates identified as Ni3X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) within the martensitic matrix, and these precipitates are responsible for age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) The rapid solidification inherent to SLM produces very fine submicron grains and a martensitic matrix in the as-built condition, which together with in-situ tempering/precipitation phenomena gives a unique hierarchical microstructure relative to conventional routes. (Tan et al. 2018)(Haghdadi et al. 2020) Prior solution treatment, aging and their combination affect the morphology and chemical composition of subsequent thermochemical layers such as nitrides. (Godec et al. 2021) Precipitation is indicated as the main factor controlling both hardness evolution and corrosion behaviour after heat treatment. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) 

### Corrosion implications
Heat-treatment-induced precipitation and microstructural changes influence corrosion behaviour, with aging often reducing corrosion potential while increasing hardness. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Reversed austenite produced by intercritical tempering was reported to raise pitting potential and lower corrosion current density and corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl compared with as-printed, aged, and homogenized samples. (Khan et al. 2022) Combining prior heat treatments with plasma nitriding yields improved wear and corrosion resistance of AM maraging steel compared with nitriding without prior heat treatment, whereas nitriding without prior aging can lead to cracks in the compound layer.
